sRoot.text: What are [[LLMs]] and how do they [[work]]?

sUse.text:
You have probably 'played' before with 
so-called [[AI chatbots]].
 (OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude, Mistral's Le Chat,...)

sUseb.text:
You have probably 'played' before with 
so-called [[AI chatbots]].

Here is a taste of it:

sUE1b.text:
> How to make pancakes?

Whisk 250g flour, 2 eggs, 500ml milk, a tablespoon of sugar, and a pinch of salt until smooth. Let the batter rest 15 minutes, then cook small ladles in a hot buttered pan — flip when bubbles form, 30 seconds more. Serve warm.

sUE2.text: > How long should I wait [[between two coats of paint]]?

sUE2b.text:
> How long should I wait between two coats of paint?

For water-based paints (acrylic, latex), 2 to 4 hours. For oil-based, plan on 16 to 24 hours. Check the can for the exact recoat window — humid or cold conditions can stretch these times.

sUE3.text: > How to list and sort [[subdirectories by size]] on Unix?

sUE3b.text:
> How to list and sort subdirectories by size on Unix?

Combine du and sort:

  du -sh */ | sort -h

'du -sh */' : reports the total size of each immediate subdirectory in human-readable form; 'sort -h' : orders those sizes naturally.

sUE4.text: > Give me [[pseudo-code to solve a simple ODE]].

sUE4b.text:
> Give me pseudo-code to solve a simple ODE.

Simplest approach is Euler's method. 

For dy/dt = f(y, t):
  t, y = t0, y0
  while t < t_end:
      y += h * f(y, t)
      t += h

Pick a small enough step h for stability; swap in RK4 for better accuracy.

sUTrans.text: [[LLM-driven artifacts]] can do impressive things and yet ...

sNextWord.text: LLMs are essentially built to do one thing: [[predict the next word]].

sNextWordb.text: LLMs are essentially built to do one thing: predict the next word. The word that follows any piece of text -- or prompt -- that is fed into them.

sNextWordc.text: LLMs are essentially built to do one thing: predict the next word. The word that follows any piece of text -- or prompt -- that is fed into them.

sGen.text: [[Decoder-style]] LLMs (such as GPT) are [[generative]] machines. They pick [[the next word]] out of a [[computed list of the most likely ones]].

sGenb.text: Decoder-style LLMs (such as GPT) are generative machines. They pick the next word out of a computed list of the most likely ones. Then the one-word-longer sequence is fed back and the process is repeated.

sGenc.text: Decoder-style LLMs (such as GPT) are generative machines. They pick the next word out of a computed list of the most likely ones. Then the one-word-longer sequence is fed back and the process is repeated, progressively generating a block of text.

sGend.text:
Decoder-style LLMs (such as GPT) are generative machines. They pick the next token out of a computed list of the most likely ones. Then the one-token-longer sequence is fed back and the process is repeated, progressively generating a block of text.

Modern LLMs mostly deal with tokens : fragments of words, rather than words directly.

sStats.text: LLMs are built through intensive [[training on huge corpora of text]] (billions of tokens).

sStatsb.text: LLMs are built through intensive training on huge corpora of text (billions of tokens). During training, they pick up statistical regularities and learn what the next token might be.

sStatsc.text: LLMs are built through intensive training on huge corpora of text (billions of tokens). During training, they pick up statistical regularities and learn what the next token might be, given what they observed in the corpora.

sNTP.text: So in a nutshell, decoder-style LLMs (such as GPT) are [[sequential next-token producers]], with [['statistical fluency']].

sMachin.text: How can a [[mechanical machine]], [[single-mindedly]] predicting the next token, generate [[fluent]] and arguably [[meaningful text]], [[answer questions]], [[write code]], [[summarize]] documents ?

sInWork.text: They do it through a handful of ideas worth unpacking: [[tokenization]] and [[embedding]] (turning text into numbers), [[attention]] (weighing context), the [[transformer architecture]] that ties them together, and [[pre-training]] — how those weights got their values in the first place.

sTok.text: [[Tokenization]]: before anything else, text is sliced into tokens — subword fragments drawn from a fixed vocabulary (on the order of 50k entries for GPT-2).

sEmb.text: [[Embedding]]: each token is then turned into a vector — a list of numbers the model can actually do arithmetic on.

sSpace.text: Each token becomes a [[vector]] — a list of numerical coordinates in a high-dimensional space. Distance in that space stands in for meaning.

sMatrix.text: A whole prompt is just a [[sequence of such vectors]], stacked row-by-row. Tokenization first turns the text into a handful of [[integer token ids]].

sMatrixb.text: Then the embedding table swaps each id for a 768-dim column. The prompt is now a 768x5 matrix of real numbers — [[this is what the model actually reads]].

sClust1.text: Project the space down to 2D and clusters emerge. [[Animal words]] land near each other -- cat, dog, fish, bird.

sClust2.text: [[Action verbs]] carve out their own region -- predict, simulate, compute, estimate.

sClust3.text: [[Statistical terms]] cluster elsewhere -- probability, variance, posterior, distribution.

sClust4.text: Even [[abstract categories]] separate cleanly: king, queen, prince, princess.

sArithm.text: Distance is only half the story: [[directions]] matter too. You can add and subtract vectors, and the results mean something.

sCap1.text: Take paris, france, germany, berlin — [[two countries and their capitals]].

sCap2.text: Start from paris. Subtract the [[france]] vector — peel off the 'country' part.

sCap3.text: Then add the [[germany]] vector — a different country.

sCap4.text: You land right next to [[berlin]]. The relation 'capital-of-country' lives as a [[direction]] in the space.

sVeh1.text: The pattern is general. Try [[plane - air + sea]].

sVeh2.text: Subtract the [[air]] vector — peel off the medium.

sVeh3.text: Add the [[sea]] vector — a different medium.

sVeh4.text: Land right next to [[boat]]. Same geometry, different meaning.

sPos.text: Word order matters. [[dog chases cat]] vs [[cat chases dog]] — same tokens, opposite meanings. But so far each token's vector stays the same wherever it sits in the prompt.

sPosb.text:
Word order matters. dog chases cat vs cat chases dog — same tokens, opposite meanings. But so far each token's vector stays the same wherever it sits in the prompt.

GPT-2 handles position with a second embedding — [[wpe]], one 768-dim vector per position — added element-wise to the wte row. The matrix stays [[5x768]], but identical tokens at different positions now carry different rows.

sAttn.text: [[Attention]]: at each layer, every token gets to look at the others and reweight them by relevance — this is the mechanism by which context shapes meaning.

sAttnBank.text: Take one ambiguous word — [[bank]] — in two sentences. Same token, same embedding row; nothing in 'bank' alone tells you which meaning is in play.

sAttnBankR.text: In the first sentence, [[fishing]] pulls hardest on bank's meaning. Arc strength is attention — the model weighs which neighbors to look at. Bank becomes [[river-bank]].

sAttnBankM.text: In the second, [[deposit]] does the same work — bank becomes [[money-bank]]. Same word, same starting vector. Different neighbors → different meaning.

sAttnBankH.text:
[[Attention heads]] are [[learned screenings]] (subspace projections) in embedding space (768d -> 64d). 

They [[learn]] to [[look for context]]: 

'bank' (a particular direction in embedding space) may be looking around for architectural details (in another particular direction), 
a noun may be looking for a qualifying adjective, 
 a premise, for a conclusion.

sAttnWrap.text:
Using multiple [[attention heads]] : screenings with different focus (syntax, semantics, logic, ...), and computing [[successive]] refinements of attention, 
token vectors [[look around]] each other and progressively [[steer]] direction in embedding space, so that the [[next-token prediction]] has extracted [['meaning']].

sTrans.text: The [[transformer]]: many attention layers stacked into a single machine that reads a next-token probability distribution off the top of the stack.

sTransEif.text: To see the stack at work, trace one token. '[[tower]]' in this sentence starts [[generic]] — the model has no idea yet which tower.

sTransEifArc.text: Early heads [[look back]] from '[[tower]]' at the distinctive attributes and [[pull them in]]. One head specializes in ' iron', another in ' old', another in ' famous'. Heads are [[narrow detectors]] — not generic searchers.

sTransEifDrift.text: Stacked across 12 layers, this pulling-in [[steers]] the representation of '[[tower]]' — away from 'generic tower', toward the region where named landmarks live. The model hasn't [[named]] the tower; but its internal encoding of it has become [[specific]].

sTransMLP.text: But [[attention]] is only half the work. After each attention block, a [[second]] block fires on the same residual: the [[MLP]].

sTransMLPBank.text: The MLP is a [[bank of learned patterns]] — roughly [[3072]] pattern-detectors, [[learned during training]]. Each one lights up for a particular kind of input.

sTransMLPFire.text: Given the contextualized '[[tower]]' vector arriving from attention, only a [[sparse handful]] of these 3072 patterns match strongly. Most stay near zero.

sTransMLPWrite.text: The firing patterns [[sum]] their outputs and [[write them back]] into the residual — adding features like '[[tall]]', '[[landmark-like]]', '[[located]]' onto '[[tower]]'. Real neurons mix many patterns; the labels here [[summarize]] what the layer's aggregate does.

sTransWrap.text: One block: [[attention]] looks around, the [[MLP]] applies patterns, the [[residual]] carries both forward. [[12 blocks]] stacked. Every [[weight]] — in every attention head, in every pattern — was [[learned]] from training data.

sArch.text: Here is the [[whole machine]] drawn as a pipeline. Token ids in at the left, a distribution over the next token out at the right — with [[embedding]], [[twelve stacked transformer blocks]], and [[unembedding]] in between.

sArchShapes.text: Sizes at each stage. Tokens come in as [[integer ids]]. Between boxes, each token is carried as a [[768-dim vector]] — that width stays constant through all 12 blocks. At the output, [[one score per vocab entry]].

sArchParams.text: Now the [[weight count]]. [[~124M parameters]] total — [[~40M]] in the embedding table, [[~85M]] spread across the 12 stacked blocks. Unembedding reuses the embedding table ([[tied weights]]) — no extra cost there.

sArchZoom.text: Zoom into [[one block]]. [[Attention]] (c_attn → Q, K, V heads → c_proj) and [[MLP]] (c_fc → GELU → c_proj) each [[read]] the residual stream and [[add]] their output back to it. Same structure, twelve times over.

sTrain.text: [[Pre-training]]: the weights are fixed by running the machine across trillions of tokens of raw text, each time nudging it to predict the next token a little better.

sTrainData.text: 'Trillions of tokens' means roughly [[a sweep of the public internet]] — web pages, books, forums, code repositories, scientific papers. The raw text humanity has written.

sTrainStep.text:
At each step: show the machine a chunk of text, hide the next token, let it guess, [[measure how wrong]] it was, then [[nudge]] every one of the [[billions of numbers]] inside the matrices a tiny bit — in the direction that would have made it less wrong. 

Repeat trillions of times.

sTrainEmerge.text:
[[Nobody designed]] the embedding clusters, the attention patterns, the steering directions. They [[emerged]] because they turned out to be useful for predicting. 

Grammar, word meaning, world knowledge — whatever helps predict the next token ends up [[encoded somewhere in the weights]].

sTrainEff.text:
What may [[appear quite mystical]]: projecting tokens in embedding space and steering them based on their neighbors 
('Doing computation on obscure vectors'),

 ends up working because such manipulations are [[tweaked until the model becomes an efficient next-token guesser]].
